opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Tasha, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how changes at work affect people's lives. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hi there, lovely to talk. I'm an independent financial adviser. Pensions, savings, helping people plan. Most of my clients have been with me for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a helpful tool, and I use it to prepare for meetings. But money is personal. People want someone they trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robo-advisers, the apps that invest for you automatically, are already taking my younger clients. That would carry on in this version, slowly. My older clients stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, but put more effort into referrals from the clients I have, like asking them to introduce their grown-up kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mildly uneasy. It's the young ones drifting off.

S0.say: It's a helpful tool, but money is personal. People want someone they trust.
S0.think: Robo-advisers, the apps that invest for you, are already taking my younger clients. My older ones stay.
S0.do: Puts more effort into referrals, asking current clients to introduce their grown-up children.
S0.feel: Mildly uneasy about the younger clients drifting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a good adviser is more than a portfolio. We're there for the divorce, the redundancy, the death in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, slow still means my client base gets older and smaller every year. In ten years, who replaces them? People my daughter's age will never think to pay someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start offering short, cheaper sessions for younger people, maybe a one-off plan instead of an ongoing fee, to get them in the door. And learn to use the AI tools to make those cheap enough to be worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A slow worry about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned divorce and redundancy. Is that from your own life too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The divorce, yes. I know what it's like to need a calm voice about money. That's why I think people will still want one.

S1.say: A good adviser is more than a portfolio. We're there for the divorce, the redundancy, the death in the family.
S1.think: Slow still means my clients get older and fewer. People my daughter's age won't think to pay someone like me.
S1.do: Offers short, cheaper one-off sessions for younger people and uses AI tools to make them affordable to run.
S1.feel: A slow worry about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say redundancy is exactly when people need a human adviser, not an app. I'd be out there saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI agents that can do routine office work can do a basic financial plan. That's a big chunk of what I charge for. The clients who need me through a crisis will stay, but the routine reviews will look expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd specialise in helping people through redundancy: payouts, pensions, what to do next. I'd partner with a local employment lawyer for referrals, cut my office costs and work more from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I can see something to aim for.

S2.say: Redundancy is exactly when people need a human adviser, not an app.
S2.think: AI agents can do a basic financial plan, and that's much of what I charge for. Crisis clients stay, but routine reviews will look expensive.
S2.do: Specialises in redundancy advice, partners with a local employment lawyer for referrals and cuts office costs by working from home.
S2.feel: Anxious, but with something to aim for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should get proper advice before they make big decisions in a boom. And the gains should reach ordinary families, not just people who already have shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed, really. My older clients would be richer on paper and my fees go up with that. But if AI is as good as a skilled adviser, the next generation won't need me at all. I'm not the best in my field, I'm a good, friendly adviser. That might not be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the most of the good years. Put more into savings, pay down the mortgage, and keep my daughter's costs covered. I'd also try to stay the human face my older clients call when they're scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Riding the good part, dreading what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd specialise in redundancy before. Does that plan still hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. There'd be loads of redundancies. But the AI could give most of that advice too. It'd be the scared, older clients who still want me.

S3.say: Get proper advice before big decisions in a boom, and the gains should reach ordinary families.
S3.think: Older clients get richer and my fees rise, but the next generation won't need me. I'm a good, friendly adviser, not the best, and that might not be enough.
S3.do: Saves more, pays down the mortgage, covers her daughter's costs and stays the human voice her older clients call when scared.
S3.feel: Riding the good part, dreading what follows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when families need to sit down and plan together. Don't panic, don't sell everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one worries me more. With hands-on jobs going too, a lot of my middle-income clients, builders, nurses, people who own small shops, start drawing down their savings just to live. Fewer savings, fewer fees. And if markets crash after the boom, I'm taking calls from frightened people every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my costs to the bone, keep my emergency fund untouched and talk to my ex about the support for our daughter. I'd keep every client I can by being there when they call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Holding it together for my clients, worried for us at home.

S4.say: This is when families need to sit down and plan together. Don't panic, don't sell everything.
S4.think: Middle-income clients like builders, nurses and shop owners would draw down savings to live. Fewer savings means fewer fees, and a crash means frightened calls every day.
S4.do: Cuts costs to the bone, protects her emergency fund, talks to her ex about support for their daughter and stays available to every client.
S4.feel: Holding it together for clients, worried at home.
